newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries crushed by busy purchasers at noon.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries crushed by busy purchasers at noon.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were nearly a point lower at noon, battered after a jump in the Chicagoland business barometer capped off a string of surprisingly robust regional purchasing managers reports, analysts said.
"There are a lot of market jitters about the national report because the regional ones keep stacking up above consensus, said Josh Stiles, senior bond analyst at I.D.E.A.

A 7.1 percent jump in the number of new single-family homes sold in May also eroded support as the market started to mull a tighter Federal Reserve policy, though probably not at Tuesday's two-day policy-setting meeting.
The long bond fell 31 points in late-morning trade, amid talk of dealers selling the September bond contract and hedge fund sales of the five-year note.
At noon, the T-bond was off 29/32 trading at 97-18/32 with a yield of 6.82 percent. The five year was down 11/32 at 99-9/32, yielding 6.42 percent.

Early weakness gathered momentum after Chicago's Purchasing Management Association reported its index rose to 61.5 in June from May's 56.8. Economists polled by Reuters had expected a reading of 57.5, on average.
At the same time, new home sales rose at an annualized rate of 825,000 units in May, well above forecasts of 786,000.
Earlier, Treasuries drifted lower after the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) released indices showing economic activity in Cincinnati and New York improved significantly in June.
The national NAPM report, due at 1000 EDT on Tuesday, will be scrutinized as the first snapshot of the economy in June.
The Fed has been banking on the fact the economy is going to cool substantially, bond experts said, adding that the housing and purchasers data did not corroborate this view.
So while it is still unlikely the market is going be expecting a tightening this week, people are more on guard for the August meeting, experts said.

"In light of Fed holding off last time and just a lot of cash piling up ... now we're repricing towards a possible 5-3/4 percent fed funds rate, which the market wasn't ready for," said a trader at a primary dealer.
"The market took their eye off the ball," the trader said.
The yield curve is expected to flatten as the front end starts to reprice, looking for a higher funds rate target before long.

Treasuries started off on a weak footing, and registered almost no reaction to a report showing a 0.3 percent rise in both personal income and spending in May. The data were close to forecasts of 0.4 percent on income and 0.3 percent for consumption.
The Fed injected an unusually large $8.651 billion of reserves into the banking system via overnight system repurchases on Monday.

Elsewhere, bills were higher before the results of the weekly auction were announced. Three-month bills were up five basis points at 5.05 percent and six-month bills were up three basis points at 5.06 percent.
